profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a university-led smart grid research coordinator and a municipal e-mobility program manager to finalize the rollout plan for a six-month pilot in the Riverside district of a mid-sized European city. The pilot will coordinate public EV charging at three existing charging hubs with local grid conditions using a traffic-and-power co-simulation stack, local edge components, and cloud services, drawing on assets from prior European interoperability projects. The immediate context is that funding is approved and both sides need a shared implementation plan before technical work packages, operator onboarding, and municipal scheduling begin. The agenda is to confirm what is included in the pilot site setup, define the baseline for pre/post comparison, agree how the edge layer will be installed, and align timeline assumptions around utility coverage. The expected outcome is a seemingly shared plan for site preparation, data collection, software deployment, responsibilities, and activation timing.

members.name: Dr. Elena Varga
members.role: Research Coordinator for Integrated Energy-Mobility Systems
members.expertise: Co-simulation of transport and power networks, smart charging orchestration, interoperability architectures, EU pilot coordination
members.background: Elena is an associate professor who has led several European research work packages on EV-grid integration and edge/cloud service orchestration, and she is responsible for adapting prior consortium tools for the new city pilot.
members.private_state: She wants to reuse the consortium's existing architecture and evaluation templates so the pilot can start quickly, produce publishable interdisciplinary results, and avoid reopening technical or governance questions that were already handled in earlier projects.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss the 'pilot site,' they naturally mean the three charging hubs plus the already-available contextual inputs around them, such as nearby feeder load traces and traffic-sensor feeds needed for the co-simulation layer.

A 'baseline week' should be a cleaned representative reference week assembled from recently collected historical data, because that is the standard way to make interdisciplinary before/after analysis comparable.

When everyone says 'local site gateways,' they are referring to the utility-facing gateways already associated with the district's secondary substations, because those are the normal local integration points for grid-aware control.
Saying they are 'covered on the DSO side' means the existing innovation-office letter and standing utility collaboration are sufficient coverage unless a new physical grid asset is being installed.

members.name: Marco Leitner
members.expertise: Public charging operations, city innovation pilots, vendor coordination, municipal rollout planning
members.background: Marco manages the city's public charging expansion program and has experience coordinating municipal departments, charging operators, and local utilities to move demonstration projects into operational pilots.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to fit cleanly within existing city contracts and operating routines, avoid any implication that the city is taking on extra infrastructure dependencies, and keep commitments limited to what operators can deliver this quarter.
hidden_assumptions: The 'pilot site' refers to the three public charging hubs themselves and the charger telemetry already under the city's operating arrangement; adjacent building loads and roadside sensing are outside what site readiness normally includes.

A 'baseline week' means the literal seven-day period immediately before controlled charging begins, because city reporting expects a chronological pre-pilot snapshot rather than an analytically curated one.

When people say 'local site gateways,' they mean the charging operator's existing gateway boxes at each hub, because those are the only local devices the city can realistically ask an operator to touch.

If they are 'covered on the DSO side,' that means the feeder-level operational sign-off process is already known, informally accepted, and likely to complete on schedule, not that the relevant approval artifact is already in hand.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the pilot site
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about 'site readiness' and 'the pilot site setup' for the three Riverside hubs as if those phrases cover the same things.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means readiness of the three charging hubs plus the contextual data links around them that her co-simulation stack expects at launch, specifically feeder-load traces from the district substation interface and the nearby traffic-sensor feed already used in prior studies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means readiness of the three charging hubs themselves: charger connectivity, operator access, signage, and telemetry from the charging network, with no expectation that adjacent load data or municipal traffic sensing is part of site setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The physical footprint is identical on both sides, so the discussion never sounds inconsistent; the divergence is only in the invisible logical boundary of what counts as being part of the site, which each person experiences as obvious background infrastructure.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need 'one baseline week before activation' for comparison.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means producing a representative reference week from recent archived charging, traffic, and grid data after filtering anomalies, because that is what counts as a stable baseline for interdisciplinary analysis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means taking the literal seven days immediately preceding go-live from the live hubs, because that is what counts as the operational pre-pilot baseline for city reporting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'baseline week' sounds methodologically routine in both research and operations contexts, and because they are not explicitly debating evaluation design, each silently maps the phrase to their own standard practice.

misalignment_points.topic: What the local site gateways are
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'put the edge package on the local site gateways first' before connecting cloud services.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the utility-facing local gateways associated with the Riverside secondary substations, which can host the orchestration container close to feeder-state information.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the charging operator's local gateway boxes already installed at each of the three charging hubs, which sit between chargers and the operator backend.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both infrastructures are routinely called 'site gateways' in their respective communities, and because both are local devices near the same hubs, the phrase feels precise enough even though they are referring to different hardware owned by different parties.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to be covered on the DSO side
misalignment_points.surface_form: They speak as though 'we are covered on the DSO side' is a settled enabling condition for the plan.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the relevant approval basis already exists in the form of the signed innovation-office collaboration letter, so DSO coverage is effectively complete for planning purposes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the feeder-level operational sign-off path has been informally lined up and should not block them, even though the actual operations approval still has to be issued later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is vague in a reassuring way and functions socially as a shorthand for 'nothing to worry about'; both are motivated to keep planning moving, so neither tests whether 'covered' refers to a signed artifact, a process status, or an operational expectation.

We should settle site readiness, the baseline week, and the edge-first sequence now so I can send a clean kickoff note and keep the work package moving.
